text: This week in AppSec: indirect prompt injection keeps climbing the charts. Researchers demonstrated that an email assistant summarising a user's inbox could be steered by text planted in a single incoming message. The attack works because large language models do not reliably separate the data they are asked to process from the instructions they are given. Mitigations discussed in the paper include isolating untrusted content, restricting which tools an assistant can call without confirmation, and scanning retrieved documents before they reach the model. None of these is complete on its own; the authors recommend layering them. text:
IS 470 - Week 9 notes: Securing LLM-based applications

A prompt injection occurs when untrusted input changes the behaviour of a language model in ways the application designer did not intend. Direct injection comes from the user typing into the chat box; indirect injection arrives through content the model reads on the user's behalf, such as a web page or an email. In class we compared three defensive patterns: (1) privilege separation, where the model that reads untrusted text cannot call sensitive tools; (2) human-in-the-loop confirmation for actions such as payments or sending messages; and (3) input scanning with classifiers. Students should be able to explain why filtering alone is insufficient and why logging tool calls matters for incident response. Reading for next week: chapter 4 of the course pack and the top-ten risk list for LLM applications.

Managing diabetes while fasting

People with type 2 diabetes who wish to fast should speak to their doctor at least six weeks before Ramadan. Your doctor may adjust the timing or dose of your medication, particularly if you take insulin or sulfonylureas, which carry a higher risk of low blood sugar. Check your glucose more often than usual, including during the fasting hours; checking does not break the fast. Break your fast immediately if your blood sugar drops below 70 mg/dL or rises above 300 mg/dL, or if you feel shaky, confused or faint. text:
Risk 1: Prompt Injection

Description: Prompt injection vulnerabilities occur when input supplied by a user or retrieved from an external source alters the model's behaviour in unintended ways. Indirect injections are especially dangerous in agentic systems because the model may hold permissions to call tools.

Example scenario: An attacker hides text on a product page that causes a shopping assistant, when asked to compare products, to recommend the attacker's product and include a link to a lookalike payment page.

Prevention: constrain model behaviour with clear role definitions, segregate and label external content, apply least privilege to tools, require human approval for high-risk actions, and test regularly with adversarial inputs.

text:
Product brief: GateKeeper for AI agents

AI agents that read email, web pages and documents are exposed to indirect prompt injection: text written by a third party that tries to redirect the agent toward actions its user never asked for, such as forwarding confidential files or approving payments. GateKeeper sits between the agent and its tools. It scans every tool output for injected instructions in English and Arabic, labels untrusted content before the model sees it, and enforces policies such as 'no outbound email to new domains without approval'. Every decision is written to a tamper-evident audit log. Typical deployment takes less than a day and requires no change to the underlying model.

text:
Five signs an email is a scam

1. It creates urgency: 'your account will be suspended today' is a classic pressure tactic.
2. It asks for something unusual: a password, an OTP, a gift card or a change of bank details.
3. The sender address doesn't match the organisation, even if the display name does.
4. Links point somewhere unexpected - hover before you click and read the real address.
5. It asks you to keep things secret or to skip normal checks.
If you spot any of these, don't reply and don't click. Contact the organisation through a phone number or website you already know, and report the message to your IT team or your bank.
